query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase high-entropy alloy (HEA), brittle behavior emerges when an intrinsic transition in deformation mechanisms occurs: the alloy loses its capacity to activate multiple, homogeneous slip systems and instead localizes deformation via stacking fault formation and incipient shear banding. This leads to stress concentration and early crack nucleation independent of grain-boundary segregation or intergranular precipitate formation typical of conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, disordered fcc high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous chemical composition and microstructure suited for high-temperature and demanding engineering service.
generation.intervention: Perform high-resolution in situ straining microscopy experiments on the HEA under controlled variations of temperature (particularly in the intermediate regime, e.g., 400–800°C) and strain rate. Compare these results to a conventional alloy that fails due to grain-boundary segregation.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under service-relevant loading conditions including intermediate temperatures where diffusion and thermally activated mechanisms become significant, and at strain rates that allow detailed tracking of slip systems activation. A direct side-by-side comparison with a conventional alloy exhibiting grain-boundary precipitation effects is required.
generation.structural_mediator: The transition from uniform multiple slip activation to localized stacking fault formation and the onset of shear banding within the single-phase matrix.
generation.mechanism: Under increasing strain at intermediate temperatures, if the intrinsic capability of the HEA to activate multiple slip systems diminishes (potentially due to thermally induced changes in local bonding or order), dislocations become concentrated and interact to form dense stacking faults and incipient shear bands. This local stress localization, rather than any intergranular effects, initiates brittle crack formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: High-resolution in situ straining microscopy will reveal that, relative to the baseline single-phase behavior at room temperature, the HEA undergoes a decline in the diversity and spatial homogeneity of slip system activation at intermediate temperatures, with a marked increase in localized stacking fault clusters and shear bands that precede crack nucleation. In contrast, conventional alloys will exhibit failure initiated at grain boundaries by segregation or precipitate-induced stress concentration.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the HEA’s behavior at room temperature, where multiple slip systems are activated uniformly leading to excellent ductility and toughness without signs of localization. Conventional alloys show brittle failure initiated at grain boundaries due to segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for service conditions at intermediate temperatures (approximately 400–800°C) and engineering strain rates. At very low or very high temperatures or under extremely high strain rates, other mechanisms might dominate, potentially limiting the observed effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold temperature or strain rate at which the slip transition occurs and the quantitative role of any local chemical or short-range ordering fluctuations in reducing slip system activity remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the single-phase HEA and a conventional alloy with known grain-boundary segregation issues. Use high-resolution in situ straining microscopy to monitor dislocation dynamics, slip system activation, and stacking fault evolution during controlled tensile tests at temperatures between 400°C and 800°C. Ensure that loading conditions (strain rate, temperature) are matched between samples.
measurements: Spatial distribution and density of activated slip systems as a function of applied strain
Formation, size, and distribution of stacking faults and shear bands
Onset and propagation of crack nucleation sites
Comparative stress–strain responses correlating with microstructural evolution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA under intermediate temperature and controlled strain rate conditions maintains a homogenous activation of multiple slip systems with negligible localized stacking fault clustering and shear band formation—resulting in ductile behavior similar to room-temperature baseline—then the hypothesis is falsified. Similarly, if crack initiation is observed to correlate with grain-boundary phenomena rather than intrinsic deformation mechanism transitions, the hypothesis would be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Such multiple deformation mechanisms inside κ phase serve to alleviate stress concentration at the phase boundary and promote uniform plastic deformation. Therefore, the simultaneous activation of unusual dislocation multiple slip and SFs in the κ phase, along with the interaction between the intersecting SFs and dislocations in the coupled L12 and fcc phases, is beneficial for enhanced strain hardening and excellent UTS and ductility. In conclusion, a strong and ductile Ni2CoFeV MEA with hierarchical order–strengthening phases is developed. This strategy effectively mitigates intergranular fracture risks in the purely ordered structures. The unique multiple deformation mechanisms contribute to extraordinary strain hardening ability and ductility. Our work provides a strategy for designing high-performance HEAs/MEAs by introducing multiprincipal-element ordered intermetallic phases in a disordered matrix, particularly promising in the Co-Fe-Ni-V system.

However, recent studies have shown that single-phase fcc high- and medium-entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) that are composed of three or more of elements Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility at intermediate temperatures (400° to 800°C) (), as summarized in Fig. 1 and fig. S1. The common feature at stress-stain curves is that these alloys exhibit strain hardening and failure shortly after the maximum tensile stress is reached. Here, we reveal the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss and provide guidelines for avoiding this problem.

reading.lever: Leverage high-resolution in situ straining microscopy to capture the transition in deformation mechanisms in a single-phase HEA, correlating slip system activation with brittleness onset.
reading.why: This approach directly distinguishes subtle mechanistic changes in deformation behavior, enabling a controlled comparison that separates intrinsic single-phase responses from conventional grain-boundary effects.
